source_acquisition.search_note: The PDF exposes only baseline/software links to ANTsX/ANTs and ITK-DReg, not an author plotting repository. Read-only gh searches for the exact title, Flash Fused Distributed Primitives, and author/method queries returned no repository or code result. OpenReview forum 8dLexnao2h was recorded in the reading but its API returned a challenge response. PDF XObject metadata names overview-fireants.pdf, scaling.pdf, and ringsampler_v4.pdf, but no public repository path is available, so no visual source file is marked source_exact.

paper_style.palette_strategy: Mechanism diagrams locally use red/coral for HBM/intermediates, blue for registers or image shards, green for shared memory/aggregates, and violet/orange for ring/halo paths. Figure 5 uses green/yellow for best/second and a separate method palette; Figure 7 uses backend-specific colors; Figure 8 uses blue/purple for on/off states. There is no stable global method color mapping and color redundancy is limited.
paper_style.vector_raster_mix: Figure 1 and Figures 5-8 have rasterized body image objects; Figures 2-4 combine embedded vector diagrams with raster subobjects. Table 1 uses PDF text, rules, and fills. The 20-page PDF has no appendix visual objects.
paper_style.style_consistency: Captions consistently use a bold Figure/Table label and compact descriptive prose; body and captions use TeX Gyre Termes/Nimbus Roman with Computer Modern math, while embedded diagram/chart text switches among sans-serif families. Figure 5 and Figure 7 have the highest density and smallest rendered labels.

figures.label: Figure 1

caption.text: Figure 1: Image Registration Problem. (a): The task is to find a coordinate transform that warps the moving image M to the fixed image F. Individual corresponding points are shown as violet arrows; the per-pixel coordinate transform is shown as a warp field φ, and the transformed image M ◦ φ. (b): A typical registration pipeline - the grid sampler warps the moving image, that is then compared to the fixed image using a loss function. Green denotes the optimizable warp, red denotes the primary bottlenecks that we optimize in this paper.

color.semantic_mapping: Grayscale MRI provides image content; violet arrows mark corresponding points; blue marks the warp-grid field; green marks the optimizable warp; red marks the grid-sampler/loss bottleneck boxes; light blue marks input/output boxes.

encodings.color: Violet arrows=corresponding points; blue warp grid; green optimizable warp; red bottleneck boxes; grayscale MRI content.
encodings.shape: Image panels, rectangular pipeline boxes, and arrow paths.
encodings.line: Solid violet correspondence arrows and solid blue/black pipeline connectors.
encodings.text: Direct labels Moving image, Fixed image, Warp field, Moved image, Grid sampler, Loss (LNCC, MI), and Backprop.

figures.data_and_statistics: Conceptual registration interface with no sample, aggregate, denominator, measured value, or uncertainty. Panel (a) shows moving/fixed/Moved images and a warp field; panel (b) shows the pipeline and backpropagation path.
figures.evidence_relation: Introduction Eq. (1) defines the transform objective; Figure 1 supplies the task and pipeline interface; §§3.1-3.3 instantiate grid sampler, LNCC, and MI bottlenecks; §4 extends the interface to GP/Ring Sampler; Figures 3-8 and Table 1 test the resulting mechanisms and workflows.
design_strengths: Task inputs, transform, output, and loss pipeline are co-located, giving the later equations and experiments a concrete interface.
Color, arrows, and direct labels separate moving/fixed/warp/moved roles without a separate legend.
The caption defines the green/red role mapping and states the bottleneck focus.
design_weaknesses: The raster body and small labels lose legibility when the figure is reduced; there is little non-color redundancy for grayscale or color-deficient viewing.
Correspondence arrows do not define coordinate direction, interpolation boundary, or a quantitative loss interpretation.
Backprop is an interface hint rather than a verifiable computation graph, and distributed state is not shown.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use a two-panel task-input/output plus computation-pipeline entry figure, with role colors defined in the caption and directional arrows; add numbered/line-style redundancy when the figure must support grayscale reproduction.

figures.label: Figure 2

caption.text: Figure 2: Left: FFDP uses fused kernels to eliminate intermediate HBM memory usage (in dark red) for memory-bound workhorse operations (grid sampler, LNCC, MI) for large-scale image registration. For grid sampler and LNCC, additional intermediate per-pixel variables (warp coordinates, patchwise statistics) are computed per-pixel in registers (blue). For MI, the Parzen Windowing and histogram aggregation is performed using shared memory (green), avoiding large HBM overheads. Right: Pie charts show the breakdown of memory overheads for storing the image, grid, optimizer state, and intermediate variables for MI and LNCC losses.

color.semantic_mapping: Dark red/coral marks HBM or materialized intermediates; blue marks registers; green marks shared memory/aggregates; orange and violet mark operation/path elements; pie sectors separate image, grid, optimizer state, interpolator, warp, step, and loss overheads.

encodings.color: Dark red/coral=HBM intermediates; blue=register variables; green=shared-memory accumulation; pie colors=memory-overhead categories.
encodings.shape: Pipeline boxes, tensor blocks, memory hierarchy triangle, and pie sectors.
encodings.line: Solid arrows/connectors show data flow and memory movement.
encodings.facet: Left: fused grid/LNCC/MI paths and kernel insets; right: LNCC and MI overhead pies.
encodings.text: Direct tensor/operator labels, memory-tier labels, percentages, and pie-category labels.

figures.data_and_statistics: The diagram compares materialized intermediates with fused register/shared-memory computation. The two pie charts encode memory-overhead composition for LNCC and MI, including image, grid, optimizer state, interpolator, warp, step, and loss categories; displayed percentages have no replicate, input-size denominator, hardware condition, or uncertainty.
figures.evidence_relation: The §3 bottleneck discussion attributes cost to deformable interpolation, cross-correlation, and mutual-information intermediates; Figure 2 maps those bottlenecks to fused kernels; §§3.1-3.3 give the implicit/fused mechanisms; Figure 7 and Table 1 measure operation/workflow resource changes.
design_strengths: Memory hierarchy, operation flow, kernel insets, and overhead composition are integrated into one mechanism overview.
The red/blue/green role mapping is repeated across the large flow and kernel panels and explained in the caption.
Pie charts make the loss/intermediate memory intuition visible without requiring the full derivation.
design_weaknesses: Small tensor labels and pie annotations are dense and difficult to read at normal paper scale.
Pie percentages lack units, input size, denominator, measurement protocol, and uncertainty, so they cannot independently be reproduced.
Color and light hatching carry most storage-role semantics and provide weak grayscale redundancy.
figures.reusable_pattern: Combine a full operation flow, focused kernel insets, and overhead composition in a single method figure; lock storage-role colors in the caption and annotate chart scale, units, and denominator next to composition plots.

figures.label: Figure 3

caption.text: Figure 3: Left: Overview of our distributed framework. GridParallel (GP) shards the fixed and moving images (F, M) and the warp field [u] across multiple GPUs. Yellow blocks and arrows denote synchronized halo boundaries between GPUs, enabling smoothing on images and warp fields without an allgather. The ring sampler (violet) computes interpolated image shards on the fly, avoiding materialization of the full moving image. We then compute losses (MSE, LNCC, MI), compute gradients w.r.t. each warp shard, apply Sobolev regularization with GP, and update shards by gradient descent. Right: Scaling efficiency compared to deep methods and CLAIRE (Mang et al., 2019), a distributed registration method. Most SOTA deep learning baselines require orders-of-magnitude more memory for the same problem size and scalability is limited to a single GPU (dotted line). Our framework scales to arbitrarily large problem sizes while using about 5× less memory than CLAIRE.

color.semantic_mapping: Yellow blocks/arrows mark synchronized halo; violet marks Ring Sampler; plot colors identify CLAIRE, SynthMorph, unigradICON, VFA, and Ours; black dotted line marks single-GPU capacity.

plot_grammar.legend_placement: inside lower-right of the right plot

encodings.x: Voxel size (×10^6) on the right log axis; no spatial x variable on the left architecture.
encodings.y: GPU usage (GB) on the right log axis; no spatial y variable on the left architecture.
encodings.color: Registration method in the right plot; halo and Ring Sampler roles in the left diagram.
encodings.shape: Circular points in the resource plot; tensor boxes and GPU rows in the architecture.
encodings.line: Solid method trajectories and a dotted capacity reference; solid arrows in the pipeline.
encodings.facet: Left: distributed framework; right: memory scaling versus voxel size.
encodings.text: GPU row labels, tensor/operator labels, method legend, axis labels, and direct mechanism annotations.

figures.data_and_statistics: The right panel positions five methods by voxel size and GPU memory on log scales and connects measurements into resource trajectories; a dotted single-GPU capacity line marks the claimed limit. The left panel is a distributed algorithm diagram. No error bars, run count, hardware accounting, or uncertainty is shown.
figures.evidence_relation: §4 defines sharded domains, GP halo synchronization, and Ring Sampler; Figure 3 left renders that distributed loop; the right plot visualizes the N/H memory-scaling prediction against CLAIRE and deep baselines; Figure 4 explains Ring partial sums and Figure 8a tests weak scaling.
design_strengths: Architecture and resource frontier co-occur, linking communication/storage mechanisms to the scale gap.
Log-log axes preserve visibility across several orders of magnitude and the dotted capacity line makes the single-GPU boundary explicit.
The caption names GP, Ring Sampler, losses, Sobolev regularization, and update steps, so the major loop is recoverable without the body text.
design_weaknesses: The caption says scaling efficiency while the visible axes are GPU usage and voxel size; the efficiency definition is absent.
Hardware conditions, repeated measurements, and uncertainty are omitted, leaving curves as unqualified point trajectories.
The dense left architecture and color-only method legend reduce readability and grayscale robustness.
figures.reusable_pattern: Pair a distributed pipeline with a log-scale resource frontier, preserving an explicit capacity reference; add the efficiency formula, hardware condition, denominator, and non-color method markers in a reusable version.

figures.label: Figure 4

caption.text: Figure 4: (a) Neighboring coordinates in the warp field may refer to pixel locations on arbitrary image shards due to the deformable nature of the warp field, making distributed interpolation non-trivial. (b) Ring Sampler interleaves fetching of image shards and aggregating the partial sums of interpolated values, avoiding a memory-expensive allgather. (c) Bilinear Interpolation is decomposed into partial sums over image shards, which are accumulated with a ring topology communication, similar to Liu et al. (2024b).

color.semantic_mapping: Panel (a) uses colored points/arrows for neighboring coordinates; panel (b) uses orange image-shard transfer, blue shard/warp, and green aggregation; panel (c) colors shard-specific partial sums.

encodings.color: Shard identity, transfer, aggregation, and coordinate categories.
encodings.shape: Colored circles/points, shard rectangles, and formula blocks.
encodings.line: Solid arrows show spatial references, ring transfers, and partial-sum accumulation.
encodings.facet: (a) random-access obstacle; (b) ring fetch/aggregate; (c) bilinear partial-sum decomposition.
encodings.text: Shard labels, Image/MΩh/[u]Ωh labels, partial-sum symbols, and direct operation annotations.

figures.data_and_statistics: Structural explanation of random-access interpolation and bilinear decomposition. Shard positions, circular sample points, arrows, and algebraic blocks encode the communication mechanism; there is no measured sample, axis, aggregate statistic, or uncertainty.
figures.evidence_relation: §4.2 moves from the random-access failure mode in panel (a) to Ring Sampler transfer/aggregation in panel (b) and partial-sum algebra in panel (c); Figure 3 uses this mechanism in the distributed loop and Figure 8a compares Ring Sampler on/off. Full correctness and derivation are called in unavailable Section I.
design_strengths: The three panels follow problem → communication operation → local algebra, making the mechanism causal and compact.
Coordinates, shard boxes, arrows, and partial sums jointly mark space and communication direction.
The caption explicitly states allgather avoidance, partial sums, and ring topology.
design_weaknesses: Tiny shard formulas and arrows become hard to read when reduced, and the figure has no separate legend or numbered key.
Shard/path colors lack line-style or label redundancy for grayscale viewing.
No communication-volume, latency, host-count, or failure-boundary annotation is shown; missing Section I limits verification.
figures.reusable_pattern: Explain a distributed random-access operator with three panels for failure mode, communication schedule, and local algebra; pair shard color with explicit IDs and add communication complexity/boundary assumptions.

figures.label: Figure 5

caption.text: Figure 5: Registration performance on Faux-OASIS dataset at 1 mm, 500 µm, and 250 µm (native 250 µm); mean ± std over pairs. ↑ higher is better; ↓ lower is better. HD90 values are reported using our cumulative definition (see Sec. K.2). (Green)/(Yellow) = best/second; † = patch-based

color.semantic_mapping: Green/yellow cell fills mark best/second; method colors identify the registration methods in panels (b,c); circle/square/triangle markers identify 1 mm/500 µm/250 µm resolutions.

plot_grammar.legend_placement: above panels (b,c), with a separate resolution key inside each plot

encodings.x: Panel (a) categorical resolution/method blocks; panels (b,c) log GPU cost (GB-hours) and wall-clock hours.
encodings.y: Panel (a) AvgDice, InvDice, and AvgHD90cum columns; panels (b,c) Dice score on a linear axis.
encodings.color: Registration method in panels (b,c); green/yellow best/second in panel (a).
encodings.shape: Circle=1 mm, square=500 µm, triangle=250 µm in panels (b,c); row/cell structure in panel (a).
encodings.line: Solid lines connect each method across the three resolutions in panels (b,c).
encodings.facet: (a) performance table-like panel; (b) Dice versus GPU compute cost; (c) Dice versus wall-clock time.
encodings.text: Method/resolution labels, metric headers, direct mean ± std values, direction arrows, green/yellow key, and patch-based dagger.

figures.data_and_statistics: Panel (a) contains 33 method-by-resolution rows (11 methods × 3 resolutions) with AvgDice, InvDice, and AvgHD90cum mean ± standard deviation over image pairs; higher is better for the first two and lower for HD90cum. Panels (b,c) reuse method colors and resolution markers to show connected accuracy-cost trajectories on log x axes. Pair count, cost denominator, hardware accounting, and graphical uncertainty are not provided.
figures.evidence_relation: §5.3 defines the simulated Faux-OASIS comparison and three resolutions; Figure 5(a) is the accuracy result, while (b,c) give accuracy-resource frontiers used for the Pareto/500× GPU-hour claim. Figure 6 is the separate real 100 µm qualitative case; faux-OASIS construction and HD90cum definition are called in unavailable Section K.
design_strengths: Exact metric values and two resource frontiers share one object, so quality and efficiency can be read together.
Resolution has marker redundancy and the caption defines mean ± std, direction, HD90cum, best/second, and patch-based rows.
The three resolution blocks expose degradation or preservation across scale rather than reporting one aggregate resolution.
design_weaknesses: The 33-row table and two trajectories make the panel dense; rasterized text and tiny legends are difficult to read at paper scale.
Method identity is mostly color-coded and the palette is not stable with Figure 7/Table 1, weakening grayscale comparison.

Cost plots have no uncertainty or denominator; the caption does not identify the comparator for the prose +18.1/+31.6/−62.1% claims, and a body cross-reference incorrectly points single-GPU capacity to Fig. 5a.
figures.reusable_pattern: Combine a precise resolution-block result table with accuracy-versus-resource frontiers, keeping direction arrows, resolution markers, and best/second semantics; add method marker/line redundancy, sample count, cost denominator, and comparator in the caption.

figures.label: Figure 6

caption.text: Figure 6: Qualitative comparison on registration of 100µm ex-vivo brain MRI (T1 → FLASH) image. Fine details like cerebellar white matter are not visible at macroscopic scales, but are aligned at 100µm. Fixed image is of size 1760 × 1760 × 1278. Best viewed zoomed in. More results in Fig. 11.

color.semantic_mapping: Grayscale MRI intensities are the image signal; red and blue boxes/connectors identify two ROI insets across the fixed, moved, and moving columns.

encodings.color: Red/blue ROI boxes and connectors; grayscale MRI intensity.
encodings.shape: Three main brain slices with paired rectangular zoom insets.
encodings.line: Solid red/blue connector lines from main slice to inset.
encodings.facet: Fixed (100 µm FLASH), Moved (250 µm → 100 µm), Moving (250 µm T1).
encodings.text: Direct modality/resolution column titles and inset structure; caption names cerebellar white matter and volume size.

figures.data_and_statistics: Single representative qualitative registration case. Columns encode modality and resolution; ROI boxes show fine structures and their zoomed views. The caption reports fixed image size 1760 × 1760 × 1278, but there is no fiducial error, overlap metric, sample count, aggregate, or uncertainty.
figures.evidence_relation: §5.2 reports the real multimodal 100 µm capability and approximately 58 s on 8 A6000 GPUs; Figure 6 supplies qualitative alignment evidence. Private fiducial annotations prevent a quantitative accuracy panel in the supplied PDF, and the caption points to unavailable Fig. 11.
design_strengths: Fixed, registered moved, and original moving states are aligned in columns with paired ROI insets for fine anatomy.
Column titles include direction and resolution, reducing modality confusion.
The caption states the qualitative finding, volume size, zoom instruction, and pointer to additional cases.
design_weaknesses: A single qualitative case has no fiducial/overlap measurement and cannot rule out local misregistration or case selection.
Thin red/blue boxes and connectors are rasterized and can blend with brain texture at small size.
No slice orientation, case ID, registration parameters, or quantitative companion is given; the additional Fig. 11 is unavailable.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use a fixed–registered moved–original moving triptych with paired ROI insets for qualitative multimodal alignment, but add case/plane identifiers and a quantitative fiducial or overlap companion.

figures.label: Figure 7

caption.text: Figure 7: Ablations on key workhorse operations: LNCC, MI, grid sampler, and scaling-and-squaring operations. Our fused kernels consume significantly less HBM and runtime.

color.semantic_mapping: Backend colors: FireANTs red, torch.compile green, VoxelMorph orange, Fast LNCC/corresponding blue, Ours purple; MI/affine/scaling panels reuse subsets for PyTorch, torch.compile, and Ours.

plot_grammar.legend_placement: at the top of each backend group

encodings.x: Voxel Size per Dimension for LNCC/MI/affine groups; Number of Steps for scaling-and-squaring/SNS group.
encodings.y: Forward Pass Time (s), Backward Pass Time (s), or Memory Usage (MB), with heterogeneous log/linear ranges.
encodings.shape: Small backend-specific point markers on connected curves.
encodings.line: Solid connected measurements within each backend curve.
encodings.facet: Four operation/backend groups × three metric panels: forward time, backward time, memory.
encodings.text: Group headings, backend legends, axis titles, voxel/step ticks, and memory/time units.

figures.data_and_statistics: Twelve small panels compare operation backends over voxel size or number of steps. Runtime is shown in seconds (often log-scaled) and memory in MB; connected points encode measured trends. The figure supplies no error bars, replicate unit, seed, hardware condition, or uncertainty definition, although the body quotes 5.22×/56.98× LNCC speedups and 50% scaling-and-squaring memory reduction.
figures.evidence_relation: The O(1) HBM and fused-gradient mechanisms in §§3.1-3.3 are tested at primitive level in Figure 7; Table 1 translates selected backends into TransMorph and FireANTs workflow outcomes. The visual supports component attribution more directly than the end-to-end comparison, but some grid/scaling claims call missing Tables/figures.
design_strengths: A fixed forward/backward/memory triplet is repeated across four operation groups, making local resource trade-offs visible.
Log runtime ranges preserve order-of-magnitude differences while memory panels retain scaling trends.
Primitive-level comparisons provide a mechanism test rather than only repeating an end-to-end score.
design_weaknesses: Twelve small raster panels and multiple legends create very high information density and tiny tick/label text.
Subplots mix x variables and log/linear ranges; the short caption does not map panels to the reported speedup claims.
No replicate or error definition is provided, and colors lack shape/line redundancy for backend identification.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use a repeated forward/backward/memory triplet for each primitive, with a consistent backend key and log runtime/linear memory views; add panel labels, replicate/uncertainty metadata, and non-color backend markers.

figures.label: Figure 8

caption.text: Figure 8: Scaling and GP ablations. (a) Weak scaling and Per-GPU memory consumption of FFDP. (b) Qualitative ablation of GP synchronization in FFDP on the fMOST mouse brain dataset (Tustison et al., 2024). Red arrows highlight regions affected by incorrect boundary effects due to no GP. See Fig. 10 for more examples.

color.semantic_mapping: Blue and purple distinguish No/With Ring Sampler in weak scaling; red arrows mark artifacts under no-GP boundary synchronization; MRI panels remain grayscale.

plot_grammar.legend_placement: top of each of the two chart panels

encodings.x: Number of GPUs for weak-scaling bars and per-GPU memory line chart.
encodings.y: Efficiency (%) in the top chart; Memory per GPU (GB) in the bottom chart.
encodings.color: Blue=No Ring Sampler; purple=With Ring Sampler; red arrows=no-GP boundary artifacts.
encodings.shape: Grouped bars, point markers, and 2×4 MRI image grids.
encodings.line: Solid memory trajectories; dashed 100% efficiency reference line; red arrow annotations.
encodings.facet: (a) weak scaling and per-GPU memory; (b) qualitative GP synchronization ablation.
encodings.text: GPU-count ticks, percentage labels above bars, chart legends, modality/resolution labels, and panel subcaptions.

figures.data_and_statistics: Panel (a) compares weak-scaling efficiency and per-GPU memory for 1, 2, 4, and 8 GPUs with and without Ring Sampler; bar labels show 100.0/98.8%, 78.2/74.0%, 74.5/62.4%, and 46.1/41.4% efficiency. Panel (b) shows fixed/moving fMOST slices under 2/4/8 GPUs with GP versus DTensor, using red arrows for boundary artifacts. No error bars, replicate count, or uncertainty is given.
figures.evidence_relation: §5.4 predicts memory independence from H with Ring Sampler and boundary correctness with GP; Figure 8a tests the Ring on/off weak-scaling prediction, while Figure 8b visualizes the DTensor/no-boundary-sync failure. Figure 3 supplies the system context; missing Figs. 9-10 are called for additional GP examples.
design_strengths: The top quantitative weak-scaling panel and bottom qualitative correctness panel test two distinct distributed mechanisms in one compact object.
Efficiency values are printed above bars and the 100% reference is explicit; MRI rows preserve the fixed/moving and GPU-count conditions.
Red arrows focus attention on the qualitative artifact regions rather than relying on a vague visual comparison.
design_weaknesses: The figure is squeezed into a single-column left block beside wrapped body text, and labels/qualitative slices are small.
Blue/purple on/off curves have limited grayscale redundancy; the caption does not describe any uncertainty or run aggregation.
The qualitative panel has no overlap metric or slice/case metadata, and additional examples in Fig. 10 are unavailable.
figures.reusable_pattern: Pair a weak-scaling quantitative panel with a qualitative boundary-correctness grid, using explicit reference percentages and arrowed failure regions; add error/replicate summaries and a quantitative correctness metric.

tables.label: Table 1

caption.text: Table 1: Accelerating TransMorph (Top) and FireANTs (Bottom) training with various computation backends.

tables.uncertainty: The TransMorph top subtable reports point values with no uncertainty. The FireANTs bottom subtable reports mean ± standard deviation for Dice and runtime and MB ± 0.0 for memory; the denominator, replicate unit, and interpretation of 0.0 are not stated.
tables.data_and_statistics: Two stacked subtables share one Table 1. Top (6 rows): Baseline/Ours × LNCC or MI × diffeomorphic ✗/✓, with Training Time (h), GPU Mem (GB), and Val DSC. Exact rows are Baseline LNCC ✗ 171.20/20.01/86.74; Ours LNCC ✗ 27.84/16.95/87.23; Baseline LNCC ✓ 171.42/21.28/86.55; Ours LNCC ✓ 27.93/17.34/87.09; Baseline MI ✗ 26.09/22.34/86.74; Ours MI ✗ 24.94/16.80/86.80. Bottom (9 rows): LNCC backends FireANTs, FastLNCC, VXM/TM, torch.compile, Ours, then MI backends PyTorch, torch.compile, Ours, torch.compile+Ours; columns are Dice Score ↑, Runtime (s) ↓, and Memory (MB) ↓. Bottom values use mean ± std for Dice/runtime and ± 0.0 for memory. Precision is mainly two decimals, with one decimal in bottom Memory.
tables.evidence_relation: §5.1 asks whether FFDP accelerates existing learned and classical workflows. The top subtable tests TransMorph loss/diffeomorphic configurations; the bottom tests FireANTs LNCC/MI backends. Figure 7 supplies primitive ablations, while Table 1 supplies workflow-level training/runtime/memory/Dice evidence; it does not isolate training-recipe and kernel effects causally.
design_strengths: Stacked workflow subtables fit learned training and classical backend comparisons into one narrow visual unit.
Headers expose loss/backend, diffeomorphic switch, units, and metric direction arrows.
The bottom subtable adds mean ± std and best/second fills, making selected Figure 7 trends numerically inspectable.
design_weaknesses: The top point values have no uncertainty, and bottom ± 0.0 memory is unexplained as measurement or rounding.
The narrow, small table requires tracking two header systems across a horizontal separator; the short caption omits Baseline/Ours, denominator, seed, and training conditions.
Best/second fills and bold are only partially redundant, and the table has no explicit cost, failure, or OOM column.
tables.reusable_pattern: Stack workflow-specific subtables in one aligned unit, with units, directions, and important switches in the headers; use the caption to define baseline labels, repetitions, uncertainty, and best/second rules.

cross_object_system.visual_narrative: Figure 1 defines registration task and pipeline; Figure 2 identifies HBM/intermediate bottlenecks; Figure 3 gives GP/Ring distributed architecture and memory scaling; Figure 4 explains Ring random-access partial sums; Figure 5 delivers Faux-OASIS accuracy and accuracy-cost comparison; Figure 6 shows real 100 µm qualitative alignment; Figure 7 decomposes resource gains into primitive ablations; Table 1 returns to TransMorph/FireANTs workflows; Figure 8 tests Ring weak scaling and GP boundary correctness.
cross_object_system.caption_system: Figures 1-4 and 6 use descriptive setup/encoding captions; Figures 3-5 also state headline directions or claims. Figure 7 and Table 1 are shorter title-plus-setup captions that leave key statistical conditions to prose. Figure 5 has the fullest direction/uncertainty key; Figure 8 combines a short top caption with panel subcaptions and a pointer to missing Fig. 10. Sample counts, hardware, repetitions, and cost denominators are not consistently captioned.
cross_object_system.table_header_system: Only Table 1 is a PDF Table. It uses two stacked subtable headers: TransMorph Top with variant/loss/diffeomorphic/training/memory/validation columns, and FireANTs Bottom with loss/backend/Dice/runtime/memory columns. Units and metric directions are explicit; Figure 5(a) is a table-like Figure panel, not a separately labeled Table.
cross_object_system.method_result_ablation_link: Figure 2's memory mechanism leads to Figure 7 primitive runtime/HBM ablations and Table 1 workflow metrics. Figure 3/4's GP/Ring interfaces lead to Figure 8 weak-scaling and boundary-artifact ablations. Figure 5 tests high-resolution simulated accuracy/efficiency, while Figure 6 supplies a real-case qualitative capability. The chain supports resource/capability claims but lacks a separate quantitative Ring-only or GP-only end-to-end table.
cross_object_system.main_appendix_link: No appendix pages are present. The body calls Sections A, D, E.1, F, G, H, I, and K plus Tables 3-4 and Figures 9-12, 19-20; these absent objects are not added to the PDF-derived inventory. Their missing content affects faux-OASIS construction, HD90cum definition, kernel gradients, Ring correctness, real-case hyperparameters, and additional qualitative examples.
cross_object_system.typography_consistency: Body, captions, and Table 1 use embedded TeX Gyre Termes/Nimbus Roman with Computer Modern math; Figures 3-4 expose Arial/DejaVu Sans or Aptos PDF text, while Figures 5-8 rasterize chart text. Figures are visually readable at 200 dpi but chart/table labels are much smaller than body text, with Figure 7 the highest density risk.
cross_object_system.color_consistency: Mechanism diagrams reuse red/blue/green/violet/orange for local storage and communication roles, but Figure 5's method colors, Figure 7's backend colors, and Figure 8's on/off colors are independent. Best/second green/yellow and most method identities rely on color, so cross-object semantic and grayscale redundancy are weak.

most_reusable_patterns: Figure 3's distributed-pipeline plus log-scale resource frontier, which places system mechanism and scale result together.
Figure 4's failure-mode → communication schedule → local algebra sequence for random-access sharding.
Figure 5's exact resolution-block result table plus accuracy-resource frontiers.
Figure 7's operation × forward/backward/memory matrix for primitive-level attribution.
Figure 6's fixed/registered-moving/original-moving triptych with paired ROI insets, when accompanied by quantitative evidence.
highest_value_objects: Figure 3 for the GP/Ring interface to memory-scaling headline.
Figure 4 for the clearest Ring Sampler random-access and partial-sum mechanism.
Figure 5 for the main accuracy, resolution, and resource comparison.
Figure 7 plus Table 1 for primitive-to-workflow resource evidence.
Figure 8 for direct Ring and GP distributed ablations.
failure_patterns: Rasterized dense panels and small embedded labels reduce legibility, especially in Figures 5 and 7.
Color carries method/backend/state identity without a stable cross-object palette or enough non-color redundancy.
Sample denominators, hardware, replicate/seed information, and uncertainty are incomplete; only Figure 5(a) and part of Table 1 provide dispersion.
Figure 6's single qualitative case leaves real 100 µm accuracy open, while referenced appendix figures/tables are absent.
A body cross-reference points single-GPU capacity to Fig. 5a instead of the visible Figure 3 scaling plot, and comparator semantics for several improvement claims are under-specified.
final_judgment.one_sentence_visual_strategy: The paper uses a concept-and-memory entry, distributed mechanism/resource frontier, high-resolution accuracy-cost comparison, primitive/workflow/communication ablations, and a qualitative real-case triptych to form a clear mechanism-to-capability chain, but pays in typography density, color redundancy, and incomplete statistical boundaries.
